gambit

GAM-bit -- two syllables, stress on the first syllable, GAM. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Gambit is a sacrificial move made to gain an advantage.

Giving away free samples all week was a gambit to draw shoppers into the brand-new store.

Worked Example

Down a goal with two minutes left, the coach pulls her own goalkeeper and sends an extra attacker forward. The net stands empty behind them -- but the swarm of attackers ties the game with forty seconds to spare.

Pulling the goalkeeper is a classic gambit: a calculated, risky move that deliberately gives something up -- a guarded net -- to gain an advantage. The word comes from chess, where a gambit offers a pawn early to win a stronger position. A gambit is bold and deliberate, never a scam and never an accident.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tactic: A tactic is any practical method for reaching a goal -- skimming the headings first, icing a sore arm after practice -- and a tactic risks nothing by itself. A gambit is a bolder kind of move: it deliberately gives something up now to win a bigger advantage later.

maneuver: A maneuver is a skillful move that changes your position -- a driver threading traffic, a general swinging troops wide. A gambit is a particular kind of maneuver: it pays a price on purpose, sacrificing something real to gain the upper hand.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

blunder: a careless, costly mistake

misstep: a wrong or unwise step

Where it sits · how much the scheme risks and spans — ploy → gambit → stratagem

ploy vs. gambit: A ploy is a move planned to outwit someone else -- a seller's ploy, a rival's ploy -- and it costs nothing to try, while a gambit raises the stakes: it deliberately sacrifices something real to win a bigger advantage.

stratagem vs. gambit: Stratagem is the strongest and grandest: a full clever scheme, sometimes with several stages, while a gambit is usually one bold opening move that sets the whole plan in motion.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — gamb

Root — gamb: leg (Italian gamba, from Late Latin gamba 'leg, hoof')

Suffix — -it

Suffix — -it: little (a worn-down form of the Italian diminutive -etto)

Put it together

Put it together: Gamb ('leg', Italian gamba) + -it ('little' -- a worn-down form of the Italian diminutive -etto) spell gambit. Italian gambetto was 'a little trip of the leg', the wrestler's move of hooking an opponent's leg. Chess players borrowed it for an opening that 'trips' the opponent by offering a pawn, and English widened it to any bold, calculated sacrifice made to gain the upper hand.

Use the root in a new word: gambol

Use the root in a new word: gambol: The lambs gamboled across the spring meadow, leaping over one another.

Root Check

Word Choice

A gambit is strategic, risky, and honest about its risk: an opening gambit, a bold gambit, a desperate gambit. It always trades something now for advantage later. Do not water it down to a mere trick or con -- a good gambit is daring, not deceitful, and the person making it accepts the cost up front.
